title: Models of Human Behaviour
position: Advanced cross-listing with NeuroAI and computational modelling
purpose: An advanced course in the Mind, Brain and AI programme, cross-listed with NeuroAI and computational modelling. Classical cognitive models, small specialised predictive models and foundation-model approaches; trial sequences, individual differences and longitudinal observations; task-, person- and time-held-out evaluation; mechanistic plausibility versus predictive fit; human-model and brain-model comparison; missing observations, privacy, and warranted versus unwarranted application claims.
description: How to build, compare and interpret models of human behaviour. Unit 1 is prepared: a complete simulate, fit, recover and evaluate loop on a two-armed bandit with synthetic participants, ending in a report with information contracts. Units 2 to 8 are outlined with their verified sources and cannot be started until they are prepared.

outcomes.description: Build the full modelling loop for a behavioural task: state competing models, simulate them, fit them by maximum likelihood, and check parameter and model recovery before interpreting any fit.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: A laboratory report with recovery results, a confusion matrix and the seed of every run.

outcomes.description: Evaluate predictive claims under a stated information contract (what is observed and predicted, what history is available, whether people, tasks or periods are new) against an appropriate baseline.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Held-out comparisons with all ten contract points stated before any number.

outcomes.description: Distinguish predictive fit from mechanistic support, and say what a fitted parameter does and does not measure about a person.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Written interpretations that label each claim and name the evidence that would change it.

outcomes.description: Assess the claims made for flexible predictive and foundation models of behaviour, and say which application claims their evaluations warrant.
outcomes.evidenceExpected: Paper-seminar reports under the programme's headings.

assessmentSpecs.title: Modelling problem sets
assessmentSpecs.description: Derivations and calculations (likelihoods, closed-form estimates, information criteria) submitted as immutable attempts with line-localised feedback; revision is expected.
rubricSummary: the model stated exactly, including initial conditions
conclusions limited to what the calculation shows

assessmentSpecs.title: Laboratory reports with information contracts
assessmentSpecs.description: Each predictive result is reported with its ten-point information contract, its baseline, its seed and its limits; predictions are saved before the runs they concern. Revision after feedback is expected.

assessmentSpecs.title: Paper-seminar reports
assessmentSpecs.description: Structured reports on the programme seminar's papers under its headings: question, model or method, evidence presented, evaluation design, baselines, important limitations, connection to earlier material, and an optional small analysis.
rubricSummary: the evaluation design stated as a contract
limitations from the paper and from its critics

provenance.authoringMethod: Unit 1 hand-authored on 2026-10-31 from the Wilson and Collins (2019) record and the course's laboratory; every number in the unit was recomputed with the laboratory code at its default seed. Units 2 to 8 are outlines that cite verified sources where they exist. Workload is estimated from unit 1 (about 6.8 hours) and the outlines.
reviewerNotes: Wilson and Collins (2019) is the spine. Its text and code differ in three ways that change numbers (initial values, the update of unchosen options, beta called a temperature in Box 4); the unit follows the code and says so.
The paper's model comparison and recovery are in-sample; the unit adds held-out comparison under an information contract, which the paper only mentions.

Centaur is cited from its Nature version of record; the CC BY arXiv preprint is the working copy that can be imported. Oh and Gobet (2026) was identified from its authors and topic; the plan that first named it was not available to the verifier.
Unit 8's coverage of missing observations, privacy and application claims has no verified source yet.

centralQuestion: How should models of human behaviour be built, compared, and interpreted?
prerequisiteGuidance: Probability, likelihood and basic model fitting (NEU-220 unit 2 or an equivalent bridge). Every predictive exercise states its information contract before any number is reported.
preparationPath: Unit 1 is prepared: the complete loop on a choice task, with its laboratory. Units 2 to 8 are outlined with their verified sources and are prepared in order; unit 8 waits for sources on privacy and application claims.
plannedActivities: Compare an interpretable cognitive model, a simple predictive baseline and a further appropriately scoped model on a modest behavioural task, stating the evaluation setting, available information, performance, uncertainty and transfer limits.
